title: Trade and honesty
hook: the honest merchant is with the prophets (Tirmidhi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, inheritance in practice, and your line: a third by will. The family's shares are fixed; the third reaches the ones they don't.

A market in Medina. Grain is heaped up for sale, dry and golden on top. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is walking past, and he pushes his hand down into the pile. His fingers come out wet. The seller says the rain got to it. Then why not put the wet part on top, the Prophet asks, so people can see it? And he says: whoever cheats is not of me. Today: trade, and the one thing a market can't run without.
screen: `A HEAP OF GRAIN IN MEDINA.` → `A HAND PUSHED INSIDE.` → `WET UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: In these texts the market isn't a dirty place. Tradition says the Prophet himself worked in trade before his mission, and the Qur'an mentions the caravans of winter and summer without embarrassment. What it watches is the scale. Surah eighty-three opens, in Pickthall's words, "Woe unto the defrauders," people who demand full measure when they buy and give short measure when they sell. Then the reward. In a report in Tirmidhi, the Prophet says the truthful, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs. Someone who sells phone cases, or tomatoes, or used cars, in that company, for telling the truth about the goods. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari makes it practical. Buyer and seller keep the right to back out until they part. If both speak truly and make things clear, their sale is blessed; if they hide things and lie, its blessing is wiped out. Two verbs: speak truly, and make clear. Not lying is half. The other half is the grain story: showing the flaw before the buyer finds it. That's why the fiqh books give buyers a right to return goods with a hidden defect the seller didn't mention. Honesty isn't left to the seller's mood; the law builds it into the contract. The honest merchant isn't a saint who wandered into a market. It's someone who puts the wet grain on top.
screen: `THE MARKET IS NOT A DIRTY PLACE.` · `WOE UNTO THE DEFRAUDERS.` · `WITH THE PROPHETS AND THE MARTYRS.` · `SPEAK TRULY, AND MAKE IT CLEAR.`

segments.voice: Replay the last thing you sold, traded or recommended: a couch online, an old phone, a pitch at work, a review you left. Was what you said true, and did the flaw get shown before anyone had to find it? No grading, just looking; if you pray, you can ask for honesty in the next one.
Trade and honesty. In Islam, trade is honorable, and a sale is blessed when both sides speak truly and make the flaws clear. Today's word.
Your line: the honest merchant. Speak truly, and make it clear. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslim merchants are taught to disclose defects, give full measure and avoid false oaths in selling, and Islamic law gives buyers a right to return goods with a hidden defect.

notes: Pickthall 83:1: confirm exact wording ('Woe unto the defrauders').
Tirmidhi 1209: confirm number and wording (truthful, trustworthy merchant with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs); grading discussed by scholars.
Bukhari 2079: confirm number; paraphrase of Hakim ibn Hizam's report.
Muslim 102: confirm number and details (rain, 'put it on top', 'whoever cheats is not of me').
'The Prophet worked in trade before his mission' is from the sira (Khadijah's caravan), not cited here; Keeper may want a source or a 'tradition says'.
Right to return goods with a hidden defect (khiyar al-'ayb): confirm general framing across schools.
